newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Europe bodies say Albania elections acceptable.
newsitem.headline: Europe bodies say Albania elections acceptable.

text.p: Top European observers of Albania's hotly-contested general election described the vote on Monday as "adequate and acceptable" and said it may lay the foundations of a stable democracy after months of unrest.

Catherine Lalumiere, the election certification officer of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), announced the preliminary verdict after receiving reports from hundreds of observers from 22 nations who monitored the first round of elections on Sunday.

"Despite minor flaws in many areas and some very serious problems in a few areas...We believe...we can say that the elections can be considered as adequate and acceptable," she said reading from a statement.
President Sali Berisha earlier conceded the defeat of his Democratic Party and the Socialist Party claimed a big win. No official results have yet been issued.
The report was signed by Lalumiere and the heads of delegations of the Council of Europe and OSCE parliamentary assemblies, Sir Russell Johnston of Britain and Javier Ruperez of Spain respectively.

The early findings were in stark contrast to what was reported after Albania's disputed general election in May last year, which the OSCE then said was marred by serious irregularities of voter intimidation and ballot stuffing.
The OSCE and Council of Europe helped Albania try to get procedures right this time, but the whole episode also served as a lesson for both the international organisations.
Lack of co-ordination between the two bodies last year meant their election reports conflicted and were seized upon by the Democrats and Socialists to suit their own political ends.
"We have learnt a lesson. There is not a point of difference between what we have to say," Ruperez told a news conference after the preliminary report was announced.

While Albania's bickering politicians were largely to blame for the political crisis, last year's performance by the OSCE and the Council of Europe muddied the election waters and to some degree contributed to the instability.
Scoring points off each other is a precarious game when dealing with a country emerging from years of dictatorship which is just beginning to understand the game of democracy.
A full, joint report by the two organisations will be issued in about two weeks' time after the completion next Sunday of run-off elections in districts where no candidate won 50 percent of the vote.
OSCE Albania envoy Franz Vranitzky secured the agreement of the two bodies for joint observer action. He had also signalled that no-one could expect the elections to be perfect.
OSCE coordination officer Tony Welch told reporters that observers were still in place at regional centres collecting the results and at the Central Electoral Commission in Tirana.
"We have received about 1,000 reports from polling stations so far. Some 88 percent of those reports rank the procedures as either good or very good," Welch said.
"In some areas, the procedures were obviously not so good but in the majority of cases this has just been ignorance of procedures...rather than done deliberately," he added.

Lalumiere ended the news conference with a message to Albanian journalists, most of whose newspapers back a political party, urging them to embrace the same democratic spirit with which the elections had been conducted.
